summary: Redwood AE/SE walked Clearview Health through rate limiting, quotas, and multi-tenant controls using org and project keys. Key discussion points: how org/project keys map to billing and quotas, per-project and per-route rate limits, emergency overrides and burst policies, RBAC and SSO integration, and considerations for Dedicated vs Hosted. Customer asked about audit logs, KMS, and tenancy isolation for pilot. Agreed next steps: pricing, docs, pilot scope, and a follow-up infra deep dive.
transcript:
[00:00] Jamie Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Jamie on the AE side at Redwood, and with me is Rohit our SE. How's everyone doing?
[00:05] Evan Rogers: Good, thanks. Busy week but excited to see how you handle multi-tenant rate limits.
[00:09] Marcus Lee: yea thanks, we were particularly interested in org/project keys and how quotas are enforced across teams.
[00:15] Jamie Chen: Great, goal for today — quick intro, demo in the Console showing org and project keys, then dive into rate limiting patterns and policies, then Q&A. We'll keep it to about 40 minutes.
[00:23] Rohit Patel: I'll share my screen now, just ping if the stream is choppy.
[00:30] [screen shared]
[02:12] Rohit Patel: Alright on screen is the Redwood Console — top left you can see the org view. We use org keys to represent a billing and policy boundary, and project keys live under orgs to map to teams/environments.
[02:27] Tanya Gomez: quick q — can a single project key have multiple rate limit policies, like route-level + global?
[02:33] Rohit Patel: Yes. You can attach a global quota at the project level and then override per-route or per-environment. Typical pattern: project global QPS for baseline, and then specific routes (e.g., /v1/generate) set a more restrictive per-second limit.
[03:02] Marcus Lee: And billing — is billing keyed to org keys or project keys?
[03:06] Jamie Chen: Billing is at the org level. Project keys are for scoping usage and applying quotas/quotas tracking — all usage rolls up to the org for invoicing.
[03:18] Evan Rogers: So if we spin up test projects for individual teams, we can cap them per-project but still show totals at org. Good.
[03:26] Rohit Patel: Exactly, and on the Console you can view token breakdowns by project and route.
[04:10] Rohit Patel: Now I'll demonstrate rate limit rules — here's the policy engine. You can define rate limits in three tiers: org-wide, project-level, and route-level. There's also a capacity tier for Dedicated customers where you can reserve X GPUs and specify burst allowances.
[04:45] [00:04:46] Speaker 1: mm-hmm
[05:00] Tanya Gomez: For encryption, we need to ensure customer-managed keys — KMS integration. Does rate limiter touch any PII?
[05:08] Rohit Patel: Rate limits are metadata — counters and logs don't contain payloads. We store counters and audit logs — the logs can be configured to redact payloads; if you're on Private or Dedicated we can use your KMS for encryption at rest.
[05:28] Tanya Gomez: okay good, need that for compliance.
[06:05] Rohit Patel: Also note we offer per-tenant isolation patterns for high compliance customers: either Dedicated pools per org or logical isolation using project keys + strict RBAC.
[06:22] Marcus Lee: How deterministic are the limits? Like do we see burst smoothing or token bucket behavior?
[06:30] Rohit Patel: It's token-bucket style with smoothing, and you can configure burst windows. We expose metrics for consumed tokens and backlog. For strict SLAs you'd pick Dedicated then we guarantee throughput up to the reserved capacity.
[07:05] Evan Rogers: If we exceed a project quota, what's the behavior? 429s, queueing?
[07:11] Jamie Chen: Configurable. Default is immediate 429, but you can enable a short grace window and automatic fallback to a cheaper model variant if you've configured a fallback policy. We also support rate-based queuing for short bursts.
[07:34] Marcus Lee: Fallback to cheaper model — is that automatic or manual?
[07:38] Rohit Patel: You define a route policy — e.g., if primary model tx-lv1 is congested or returns a 503, route to tx-lv0 with lower cost and slightly worse quality. It's part of smart routing.
[08:01] [08:01] Speaker 2: okay
[08:12] Jamie Chen: Quick note on org/project keys lifecycle — keys can be rotated, revoked, and annotated. You can tag keys with environment, owner, and TTL. We also have project-level quotas that can be bumped temporarily via the Console or API by admins.
[08:37] Tanya Gomez: For audit purposes, can we get per-request metadata with which key called it?
[08:42] Rohit Patel: Yes, request headers include key ID and you can ship the logs to your logging endpoint or S3. We surface that in audit logs; again you can redact bodies.
[09:10] Rohit Patel: I'll switch to the API example — here's a sample curl that sets a project-level limit via the Management API. (shows code). The API supports granular rules and rate windows in seconds/minutes.
[09:45] Marcus Lee: Is there an SDK? Our platform is Python heavy.
[09:49] Rohit Patel: Yep we have python and node SDKs and CLI tooling — you can configure policies and create keys from infra as code.
[10:20] [10:20] Dr. Priya Nair: we want to control per-customer SLAs inside our tenant — can we map sub-customers to projects?
[10:28] Jamie Chen: You can either create projects per sub-customer or use tagging and duplicate policies. Projects are the recommended boundary.
[10:36] Rohit Patel: One thing customers do is create a project per environment (prod, staging) and then sub-projects per external customer; then RBAC enforces who can rotate keys.
[11:05] Evan Rogers: There's concerns about noisy neighbors — how do you protect production traffic from a misbehaving project?
[11:12] Rohit Patel: Route-level caps and priority queuing. Also, organization admins can set hard caps that apply across the entire org to prevent overconsumption. For Dedicated deployments, isolation at the GPU pool level is the best approach.
[11:35] [11:35] Rohit Patel: Now I'm going to simulate a high QPS burst against /v1/generate to show enforcement.
[11:45] [live demo: burst test]
[12:20] Rohit Patel: You can see the metrics — tokens/sec spike, then the limiter clamps and we start returning 429s for the offending project while others remain healthy.
[12:34] Marcus Lee: Nice, can we set alerts on when a project hits 80% of quota?
[12:39] Rohit Patel: Yep — alerting and webhooks are built into console. You can also export metrics into Datadog or CloudWatch.
[13:05] Tanya Gomez: About logs and retention — we need 7 years of audit for certain flows — is that possible?
[13:12] Jamie Chen: On Hosted we have standard retention windows but offer extended retention as an add-on. Private/Dedicated deployments give you control over retention, and you can archive to your S3 via the log export.
[13:39] Rohit Patel: Quick aside on quotas vs spending limits — spending limits stop token consumption from being billed but don't necessarily stop requests; quotas are intended for hard caps. We recommend using both: quota for technical enforcement, spending limits for cost guardrails.
[14:05] Evan Rogers: For our pilot, we want to measure latency and cost per request under our typical mix, and also see enforcement behavior.
[14:12] Jamie Chen: Perfect — we'll run a small benchmark with your routes and show token breakdowns and per-route latency percentiles.
[14:25] [14:25] Speaker 3: thanks
[15:00] Rohit Patel: Now a bit on RBAC and SSO — we support SAML/Okta, and Console roles map to org admin, billing-only, project-admin, and read-only. Project admins can rotate keys and adjust quotas for their projects.
[15:28] Tanya Gomez: Will project-admins be able to exfiltrate keys? Concern about lateral movement.
[15:33] Rohit Patel: Good question — project-admins can manage keys for their projects only. Cross-project key ops require org-admin. We can also enable approval workflows for key rotation if you need multi-person control.
[15:56] Marcus Lee: Are there change logs for key rotations?
[15:59] Rohit Patel: Yes all key lifecycle events appear in audit logs with actor info and IP.
[16:25] Rohit Patel: Back to Dedicated vs Hosted: Dedicated gives you reserved throughput and optional VPC/private control plane — lower noisy neighbor risk and stronger data isolation. Hosted is faster to get started and you get Redwood-managed uptime and upgrades.
[16:50] Evan Rogers: If we go Dedicated for pilot, can we start Hosted then migrate?
[16:55] Jamie Chen: Yes, migration paths exist. We can seed Dedicated from your existing projects and keys; some network work for VPC peering but it's a common pattern.
[17:12] Dr. Priya Nair: Hey quick product question — do you do per-project model quantization settings? Some teams want different latency/cost tradeoffs per project.
[17:21] Rohit Patel: You can set model profiles per project — choose quantized variants for cost-sensitive projects and full-precision for high-quality ones. The routing and fallback rules then choose the appropriate variant.
[17:45] [17:45] Speaker 4: ok
[18:02] Jamie Chen: We've touched on performance — now policy enforcement examples: rate limiting at 100 QPS project-level, route-level 20 QPS for /v1/embedding, fallback to cheaper model when quota reached, and emergency override via org-admin which can be audited.
[18:30] Marcus Lee: Are overrides logged and reversible?
[18:33] Rohit Patel: Yes, every override is an auditable event and has a TTL so it auto-reverts unless extended.
[18:50] Evan Rogers: Can alerts trigger automatic mitigation like temporarily blocking a misbehaving project?
[18:55] Rohit Patel: Yes, automation rules can be configured: if error rate > X and quota > Y, block key and notify org-admins.
[19:20] [19:20] Rohit Patel: I'm going to show the API call pattern for creating a project key with a hard quota and webhook for alerts. (displays curl)
[19:45] Marcus Lee: The webhook — does that include sample payloads for 429s?
[19:49] Rohit Patel: It includes key id, route, timestamp, and metric snapshot — not full request body.
[20:10] Tanya Gomez: For PKI and key storage — are keys stored encrypted?
[20:14] Rohit Patel: Keys are encrypted at rest; for customers using our Private offering we support customer-managed encryption keys (bring-your-own-kms).
[20:40] [20:40] Jamie Chen: Let's talk about SLOs — Hosted customers get a published availability SLO; Dedicated can opt into contractual SLAs with credits.
[20:55] Evan Rogers: We'll likely need a contractual SLA for the pilot if we use it for production.
[21:01] Jamie Chen: Noted — I'll include SLA options in the quote.
[21:20] Rohit Patel: Quick note on testing: we can run a proof-of-concept in our sandbox with production-like load and share dashboards. It usually lasts 2-4 weeks.
[21:35] Marcus Lee: Any limitations on number of project keys? We may want a lot for microservices.
[21:40] Rohit Patel: No hard limit — we recommend grouping where it makes sense. Keys are lightweight objects.
[22:05] [22:05] Rohit Patel: I'll run through edge cases — if you have long-running streaming requests they consume concurrency differently; we rate by active streams and token throughput.
[22:30] Dr. Priya Nair: For streaming, can we set different limits?
[22:34] Rohit Patel: Yes streaming limits are separate and you can cap concurrency.
[23:00] Jamie Chen: Want to cover a couple customer-specific concerns — Tanya, you flagged audit retention and KMS. We'll attach our security pack and SOC2 artifacts.
[23:15] Tanya Gomez: Thanks, please include data residency notes — some PII must remain in-region.
[23:21] Rohit Patel: For Hosted we have region options; Dedicated/Private gives you full control over region and data plane.
[23:40] Evan Rogers: Ok timeline question — we are aiming for a pilot in August. What do you need from us?
[23:47] Jamie Chen: Ideally a list of routes and expected QPS, contact for security questionnaire, and a pilot success criteria doc. We'll turn around pricing and a pilot plan.
[24:05] [24:05] Speaker 5: thanks
[24:30] Rohit Patel: I'll show the admin screen for creating an emergency override now — here you can set TTL, reason, and it's audited.
[25:05] Rohit Patel: Demo complete — I'll stop sharing.
[25:12] Jamie Chen: Great — let's open for questions.
[25:18] Marcus Lee: A question on multi-region failover — if one region is saturated, can we failover requests to another region automatically?
[25:25] Rohit Patel: Yes, smart routing supports region fallback based on latency and capacity. For cross-region failover make sure models are available in both regions or fallback to compatible variants.
[25:44] Marcus Lee: Do you replicate KV caches across regions?
[25:48] Rohit Patel: KV caches are per-region; we rely on shorter TTLs and warm-start strategies for multi-region setups.
[26:10] Tanya Gomez: On access controls — can we restrict which IPs can call a project key?
[26:16] Rohit Patel: Yes you can set IP allowlists on keys and enforce mutual TLS for extra security.
[26:35] Evan Rogers: Anything else we should be aware of for cost control?
[26:40] Rohit Patel: Use token budgeting per project, prefer quantized models for bulk work, and enable cached prefix reuse where applicable. Our Optimize tool provides recommendations.
[27:10] [27:10] Jamie Chen: Quick recap of decisions and next steps — we'll send pricing and SLA options, demo recording, org/project keys guide, and a proposed pilot plan. Customer provides QPS/routes and security contacts.
[27:30] Dr. Priya Nair: sounds good.
[28:00] Evan Rogers: One last thing on legal — we need a data processing addendum (DPA) and indemnities for healthcare data.
[28:08] Jamie Chen: We'll include the DPA in the materials and loop in Legal.
[28:20] Marcus Lee: Thanks, also can you share an example webhook payload and the alerting thresholds you used in the demo?
[28:27] Rohit Patel: Yes, included in the doc pack I'll share.
[28:45] Tanya Gomez: For pilot success metrics — recommend we measure 95th latency, error rate, and cost per 1k tokens.
[28:53] Jamie Chen: Agreed and we'll annotate the pilot plan with those KPIs.
[29:10] [29:10] Speaker 6: thanks
[29:40] Jamie Chen: Alright we'll summarize by email and share the recording and docs. Any final questions?
[29:48] Marcus Lee: none from me.
[29:51] Evan Rogers: same.
[30:00] Jamie Chen: Great, thanks everyone — look out for the follow-up.
[30:05] [call ends — recording stops]
